q: Which layer of the heart wall is also called the visceral layer of the serous pericardium?
o: Endocardium
Fibrous pericardium
Parietal pericardium
Epicardium
w: The epicardium is the visceral layer of the serous pericardium: it lies directly on the heart's surface, with pericardial fluid between it and the parietal layer.

n.0: The endocardium lines the chambers and valves on the inside of the heart.
n.1: The fibrous pericardium is the tough outermost sac, not a serous layer on the heart.
n.2: The parietal pericardium lines the inside of the fibrous sac; visceral means on the organ itself.

q: The first heart sound, S1 ("lub"), is produced by which event in the cardiac cycle?
o: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the start of diastole
Closure of the tricuspid and mitral valves as ventricular systole begins
Opening of the aortic and pulmonary valves as the ventricles eject
Contraction of the atria at the end of ventricular filling
w: S1 ("lub") is the sound of the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and mitral) closing as the ventricles begin to contract. S2 ("dub") is the semilunar valves closing.

n.0: Closure of the semilunar valves at the start of diastole produces S2 ("dub"), not S1.
n.2: Normal heart sounds come from valves closing, not opening.
n.3: Atrial contraction tops up ventricular filling but is not the source of S1.

q: Which valve lies between the heart chamber with the thickest myocardium and the largest artery of the body?
o: Tricuspid valve
Aortic semilunar valve
Pulmonary semilunar valve
Mitral (bicuspid) valve
w: The left ventricle has the thickest myocardium, and the aorta is the largest artery. The aortic semilunar valve guards the exit from the left ventricle into the aorta.

n.0: The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and the right ventricle.
n.2: The pulmonary valve guards the exit from the thinner-walled right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk.
n.3: The mitral valve sits at the entrance to the left ventricle, between it and the left atrium, not at its exit.

q: Which statement correctly describes the position of the heart in the thorax?
o: It lies in the left pleural cavity with its apex pointing up and to the left
It lies in the mediastinum with its apex pointing down and to the left
It lies in the mediastinum with its base resting downward on the diaphragm
It lies in the mediastinum with its apex pointing up and to the right
w: The heart sits in the mediastinum between the lungs, enclosed in the pericardial cavity, with its apex pointing down, forward and to the left.

n.0: The pleural cavities surround the lungs; the heart is in the mediastinum, and its apex points down.
n.2: The broad base faces up and back toward the great vessels; the apex is the part that points down.
n.3: The apex points down and to the left, not up and to the right.

q: The atrioventricular valve with three cusps opens, and blood moves from one chamber into another. Which chamber is receiving the blood?
o: Left ventricle
Right atrium
Pulmonary trunk
Right ventricle
w: Step 1: the AV valve with three cusps is the tricuspid valve, on the right side. Step 2: AV valves let blood pass from atrium to ventricle, so the right ventricle is receiving blood from the right atrium.

n.0: The left ventricle receives blood through the mitral (bicuspid) valve, which has two cusps.
n.1: The right atrium is the chamber sending blood through the tricuspid valve, not receiving it.
n.2: The pulmonary trunk receives blood through the pulmonary semilunar valve, not an AV valve.

q: An infant has a congenital opening that lets oxygenated blood pass from the left ventricle straight into the right ventricle. Which structure has the defect?
o: The interatrial septum
The tricuspid valve
The mitral (bicuspid) valve
The interventricular septum
w: The interventricular septum is the muscular wall between the right and left ventricles; it normally keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood apart, so an opening in it (a ventricular septal defect) lets blood cross from the left ventricle to the right.

n.0: The interatrial septum separates the two atria; an opening there lets blood pass between the atria, not the ventricles.
n.1: The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle; it does not connect the two ventricles.
n.2: The mitral valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle; a faulty mitral valve lets blood leak back into the left atrium, not into the right ventricle.

q: Which three arteries branch directly from the arch of the aorta?
o: Brachiocephalic, right subclavian, left subclavian
Brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian
Right and left common carotid, brachiocephalic
Right and left coronary, brachiocephalic
w: The aortic arch gives off three branches: the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery and the left subclavian artery. The right common carotid and right subclavian arteries arise from the brachiocephalic trunk.

n.0: The right subclavian also comes off the brachiocephalic trunk; only the left subclavian leaves the arch directly.
n.2: The right common carotid branches from the brachiocephalic trunk, not directly from the arch.
n.3: The coronary arteries branch from the base of the ascending aorta just above the aortic valve, before the arch.

q: A vessel carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Which statement about this vessel is correct?
o: It is an artery, and its blood is low in oxygen
It is a vein, and its blood is rich in oxygen
It is a vein, and its blood is low in oxygen
It is an artery, and its blood is rich in oxygen
w: Arteries are defined by direction: they carry blood away from the heart, whatever its oxygen content. The pulmonary arteries carry blood from the right ventricle to the lungs before gas exchange, so they are arteries carrying oxygen-poor blood.

n.1: A vessel carrying blood away from the heart is an artery, and blood on its way to the lungs is oxygen-poor.
n.2: Low oxygen does not make a vessel a vein; vessels are named by direction, and this one carries blood away from the heart.
n.3: It is an artery, but blood leaving the right ventricle has returned from the body and has not yet picked up oxygen in the lungs.

q: When the right ventricle contracts, blood leaves it through which valve and enters which vessel?
o: The pulmonary valve, into the pulmonary trunk
The aortic valve, into the aorta
The pulmonary valve, into the pulmonary veins
The tricuspid valve, into the pulmonary trunk
w: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary (semilunar) valve into the pulmonary trunk, which divides into the pulmonary arteries to the lungs.

n.1: The aortic valve and aorta are the exit route from the left ventricle.
n.2: Pulmonary veins return blood from the lungs to the left atrium; they do not connect to the right ventricle.
n.3: The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle, at the entrance to the ventricle, not its exit.

q: The systemic circulation begins in which chamber of the heart, and to which chamber does it return blood?
o: It begins in the right ventricle and returns blood to the left atrium
It begins in the left ventricle and returns blood to the right atrium
It begins in the left atrium and returns blood to the right ventricle
It begins in the left ventricle and returns blood to the left atrium
w: Systemic circulation: left ventricle to aorta, body tissues and venae cavae, ending in the right atrium. Pulmonary circulation runs from the right ventricle to the lungs and back to the left atrium.

n.0: Right ventricle to left atrium describes the pulmonary circulation.
n.2: Atria receive blood rather than pump it into a circuit; the systemic circuit starts at the left ventricle.
n.3: Systemic blood returns through the venae cavae to the right atrium, not the left.

q: The coronary arteries supply oxygenated blood to the myocardium. From which vessel do they branch?
o: The coronary sinus, on the back of the heart
The superior vena cava, where it enters the right atrium
The base of the aorta, directly above the aortic valve
The pulmonary trunk, directly above the pulmonary valve
w: The right and left coronary arteries branch from the base of the aorta directly above the aortic valve. They fill mainly during diastole.

n.0: The coronary sinus is a vein that collects blood from the heart muscle and drains it into the right atrium.
n.1: The superior vena cava carries deoxygenated blood into the right atrium.
n.3: The pulmonary trunk carries deoxygenated blood, which could not supply the myocardium.

q: After a meal, blood carrying absorbed nutrients from the small intestine travels first to which organ before returning to the heart?
o: The kidneys, through the renal veins
The liver, through the hepatic artery
The liver, through the hepatic veins
The liver, through the hepatic portal vein
w: Blood from the stomach, intestines, spleen and pancreas drains into the hepatic portal vein, which takes it to the liver for processing before it reaches the inferior vena cava and the heart.

n.0: Renal veins drain the kidneys, not the intestine.
n.1: The hepatic artery brings oxygenated blood from the aorta to the liver; it does not carry blood from the intestine.
n.2: The hepatic veins carry blood out of the liver into the inferior vena cava; intestinal blood enters the liver through the hepatic portal vein.

q: In a fetus, the umbilical vein carries blood from the placenta to the fetus. Based on how veins are defined, which statement is correct?
o: It carries deoxygenated blood toward the fetal heart
It carries oxygenated blood toward the fetal heart
It carries oxygenated blood away from the fetal heart
It carries deoxygenated blood away from the fetal heart
w: Step 1: a vein carries blood toward the heart. Step 2: blood leaving the placenta has picked up oxygen, so the umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood toward the fetal heart (the umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood away).

n.0: Blood coming from the placenta has just been oxygenated there.
n.2: Carrying blood away from the heart would make it an artery.
n.3: This describes the umbilical arteries, which return deoxygenated blood to the placenta.

q: A red blood cell leaves the left ventricle, travels to a capillary in the big toe and eventually returns to the left ventricle. Which capillary beds does it pass through, and in what order?
o: Two beds: the toe, then the pulmonary capillaries
Three beds: the toe, the coronary bed, then the lungs
Two beds: the pulmonary capillaries, then the toe
One bed: the systemic capillaries in the toe
w: Step 1: from the left ventricle the cell goes through systemic arteries to the toe capillaries, then back by veins to the right atrium. Step 2: the right ventricle sends it to the pulmonary capillaries, and the pulmonary veins return it to the left atrium and left ventricle. Two beds, systemic first.

n.1: The coronary bed is a separate branch of the systemic circuit, not a stop on the route to and from the toe.
n.2: Leaving the left ventricle, it enters the systemic circuit first; the lungs come after the right ventricle.
n.3: To get back to the left ventricle it must also pass through the lungs, a second capillary bed.

q: A blood sample is drawn from a pulmonary artery and compared with a sample from a pulmonary vein. How does the pulmonary artery sample differ?
o: It has the same oxygen, since both vessels serve the lungs
It has higher oxygen and lower carbon dioxide
It has higher oxygen and higher carbon dioxide
It has lower oxygen and higher carbon dioxide
w: Step 1: the pulmonary artery carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, before gas exchange. Step 2: the pulmonary vein carries blood after exchange. So the arterial sample is lower in O₂ and higher in CO₂ (the classic exception to the oxygen rule).

n.0: Gas exchange in the lung capillaries lies between the two vessels, so their oxygen content differs.
n.1: This would be true of a systemic artery compared with a systemic vein, but the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood.
n.2: Blood that is high in CO₂ has not yet unloaded it in the lungs, so its O₂ is low as well.

q: Blood leaving the brain returns to the heart. Which sequence of vessels and chamber is correct?
o: Jugular veins, inferior vena cava, right atrium
Jugular veins, superior vena cava, left atrium
Carotid arteries, superior vena cava, right atrium
Jugular veins, superior vena cava, right atrium
w: Veins carry blood toward the heart. The jugular veins drain the head and neck into the superior vena cava (by way of the brachiocephalic veins), which empties into the right atrium.

n.0: The inferior vena cava drains the body below the diaphragm; blood from the head reaches the heart through the superior vena cava.
n.1: The venae cavae empty into the right atrium; the left atrium receives the pulmonary veins.
n.2: The carotid arteries carry blood to the head, away from the heart; the return route is venous.

q: Which structure in the wall of the heart normally acts as its natural pacemaker, setting a resting rate of about 60 to 100 impulses per minute?
o: Purkinje fibers
Sinoatrial (SA) node
Bundle of His (AV bundle)
Atrioventricular (AV) node
w: The sinoatrial (SA) node, in the wall of the right atrium, fires fastest (about 60 to 100 impulses per minute), so it sets the pace for the whole heart.

n.0: Purkinje fibers spread the impulse through the ventricles; their own intrinsic rate is much slower than the SA node's.
n.2: The bundle of His conducts the impulse from the AV node into the septum; it does not set the rate.
n.3: The AV node can take over as a backup pacemaker, but it fires more slowly than the SA node, so it does not normally set the rate.

q: Why does the electrical impulse pause briefly at the atrioventricular (AV) node before passing to the ventricles?
o: To let the atria refill with blood before they contract again
To let the SA node reset before it fires the next impulse
To let the semilunar valves close before the atria contract
To let the ventricles fill with blood before they contract
w: The AV node delay gives the atria time to finish contracting and push blood into the ventricles, so the ventricles are full before they contract.

n.0: The atria refill during ventricular systole and diastole; the AV delay serves ventricular filling.
n.1: The SA node's timing does not depend on the AV node delay; the delay is about ventricular filling.
n.2: The semilunar valves close at the end of ventricular systole, not before atrial contraction.

q: A nursing student is reading a normal electrocardiogram (ECG) tracing. Which electrical event does the P wave represent?
o: Atrial depolarization
Atrial repolarization
Ventricular depolarization
Ventricular repolarization
w: The P wave is atrial depolarization, which triggers atrial contraction. The QRS complex is ventricular depolarization and the T wave is ventricular repolarization.

n.1: Atrial repolarization is hidden within the QRS complex and has no separate wave.
n.2: Ventricular depolarization is the QRS complex.
n.3: Ventricular repolarization is the T wave.

q: A client's heart rate rises from 70 to 90 beats per minute while stroke volume falls from 80 mL to 70 mL per beat. What happens to cardiac output?
o: It rises, from 5.6 to 7.2 L/min
It stays at 5.6 L/min, as the changes offset
It falls, from 5.6 to 4.9 L/min
It rises, from 5.6 to 6.3 L/min
w: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. Before: 70 × 80 mL = 5,600 mL/min (5.6 L/min). After: 90 × 70 mL = 6,300 mL/min (6.3 L/min). Output rises.

n.0: 7.2 L/min is 90 × 80 mL: it applies the new heart rate but keeps the old stroke volume of 80 mL.
n.1: Cardiac output is a product, not a sum: the rise in rate (× 90/70) outweighs the fall in stroke volume (× 70/80).
n.2: 4.9 L/min is 70 × 70 mL: it applies the new stroke volume but keeps the old heart rate of 70.

q: Atrial repolarization does not appear as a separate wave on a normal ECG. Why?
o: It occurs during the QRS complex and is hidden by it
It occurs during the T wave and is hidden by it
It occurs after the T wave and is too small to record
It occurs during the P wave and is hidden by it
w: The atria repolarize at about the same time the ventricles depolarize, so the small atrial repolarization signal is masked by the much larger QRS complex.

n.1: The T wave is ventricular repolarization, which happens later, while the atria are already at rest.
n.2: After the T wave the whole heart is at rest; the atria repolarized much earlier.
n.3: The P wave is atrial depolarization; repolarization cannot occur at the same moment.

q: Cardiac muscle is autorhythmic. Which statement best describes the role of the autonomic nervous system in heart rate?
o: It sets the rhythm: the medulla sends one impulse to the ventricles per beat
It adjusts the rate: sympathetic nerves speed it and the vagus nerve slows it
It adjusts the rate: the vagus nerve speeds it and sympathetic nerves slow it
It starts each beat: sympathetic nerves fire the SA node with each heartbeat
w: The SA node generates each beat without nerve input. The autonomic nervous system only changes the rate: sympathetic stimulation speeds it up and parasympathetic (vagus) stimulation slows it.

n.0: The medulla's cardiac center adjusts autonomic output, but the impulse for each beat comes from the SA node.
n.2: The roles are reversed: the vagus (parasympathetic) slows the heart and sympathetic nerves speed it.
n.3: The SA node fires on its own (autorhythmicity); nerves modify the rate but do not trigger each beat.

q: After the impulse passes through the AV bundle (bundle of His), which structures does it travel through next?
o: The atrioventricular node
The bundle branches
The Purkinje fibers
The sinoatrial node
w: Conduction runs SA node, AV node, AV bundle (bundle of His), right and left bundle branches in the interventricular septum, then Purkinje fibers in the ventricular walls.

n.0: The AV node comes before the bundle of His; it delays the impulse so the ventricles can fill.
n.2: The Purkinje fibers come after the bundle branches; they spread the impulse through the ventricular myocardium.
n.3: The SA node starts each impulse in the wall of the right atrium, at the very beginning of the pathway.

q: A clinic records an adult's blood pressure as 118/76 mmHg. What does the 76 represent?
o: Arterial pressure while the ventricles contract (systolic pressure)
Arterial pressure while the ventricles relax (diastolic pressure)
Arterial pressure while the atria contract at the end of filling
Venous pressure while the ventricles relax and fill with blood
w: Blood pressure is written systolic/diastolic. The lower number (76) is the diastolic pressure in the arteries while the ventricles relax and fill.

n.0: Systolic pressure, during ventricular contraction, is the top number (118).
n.2: Diastolic pressure is the minimum arterial pressure during ventricular relaxation; it is not defined by atrial contraction.
n.3: A blood pressure cuff measures arterial pressure, not venous pressure.

q: Which pairing of a common pulse or blood pressure site with its artery is correct?
o: Top of the foot: popliteal artery
Back of the knee: femoral artery
Front of the elbow: radial artery
Front of the elbow: brachial artery
w: The brachial artery runs through the antecubital region (front of the elbow), where blood pressure is usually measured. The radial artery is felt at the wrist, the popliteal artery behind the knee and the dorsalis pedis on top of the foot.

n.0: The pulse on top of the foot is the dorsalis pedis; the popliteal artery lies behind the knee.
n.1: The artery behind the knee is the popliteal; the femoral pulse is felt in the groin.
n.2: The radial artery gives the wrist pulse; at the front of the elbow the artery is the brachial.

q: A nursing student labels a normal ECG strip. Which wave follows the QRS complex, and what does it represent?
o: T wave; atrial repolarization
P wave; ventricular repolarization
T wave; ventricular contraction
T wave; ventricular repolarization
w: After the QRS complex (ventricular depolarization) comes the T wave, which records ventricular repolarization as the ventricles recover before the next beat.

n.0: Atrial repolarization is hidden within the QRS complex; the T wave is ventricular repolarization.
n.1: The P wave comes before the QRS complex and shows atrial depolarization.
n.2: Ventricular contraction follows depolarization, shown by the QRS complex; the T wave is the electrical recovery.

q: Gases, nutrients and wastes are exchanged between blood and tissues in capillaries rather than in arteries or veins. Which feature of capillaries makes this possible?
o: Their wall has all three tunics, each thinned to one cell
Their wall is a single layer of endothelial cells
Their wall is a thin tunica media with no inner lining
Their wall is a single layer of cuboidal epithelial cells
w: A capillary wall is a single layer of endothelium (simple squamous epithelium), giving a very short diffusion distance. Blood also flows slowest in capillaries, allowing time for exchange.

n.0: Capillaries lack the tunica media and tunica externa; only the endothelial layer of the tunica intima remains.
n.2: Capillaries have no tunica media (smooth muscle); their wall is the endothelium of the tunica intima alone.
n.3: Capillary walls are one cell thick, but the cells are flat (simple squamous) endothelium; cuboidal cells would lengthen the diffusion distance.

q: Blood in the veins of the legs is under low pressure, yet it returns upward to the heart. Which features make this possible?
o: Narrow lumens that raise the pressure inside them
Elastic walls that recoil after each heartbeat
One-way valves aided by the skeletal muscle pump
Thick smooth-muscle walls that pump blood upward
w: Veins have one-way valves, and contracting leg muscles squeeze the veins (the skeletal muscle pump), pushing blood toward the heart while the valves prevent backflow.

n.0: Veins have large lumens and low pressure; narrow lumens describe arterioles.
n.1: Elastic recoil after each beat is a feature of large arteries, not veins.
n.3: Veins have thinner walls with less smooth muscle than arteries, and they do not pump.

q: A lab technician examines a stained blood smear from a healthy adult. Which description fits a mature red blood cell?
o: Biconcave disc with no hemoglobin that lives about 120 days
Biconcave disc with a nucleus that lives about 120 days
Biconcave disc with no nucleus that lives about 120 days
Spherical cell with no nucleus that lives about 120 hours
w: Mature red blood cells are biconcave discs, lose their nucleus so they can pack in more hemoglobin, and circulate for about 120 days before macrophages in the spleen and liver remove them.

n.0: Mature RBCs are packed with hemoglobin, the iron-containing protein that carries oxygen; losing the nucleus makes room for more of it.
n.1: Mature RBCs have no nucleus; they lose it during development.
n.3: RBCs are biconcave, not spherical, and they live about 120 days, not 120 hours.

q: Which white blood cell is the largest in normal blood and leaves the bloodstream to become a macrophage in the tissues?
o: Lymphocyte
Neutrophil
Monocyte
Basophil
w: Monocytes are the largest leukocytes. They circulate briefly, then enter the tissues and develop into macrophages, long-lived phagocytes that also present antigens.

n.0: Lymphocytes (B, T and NK cells) drive specific and antiviral defense; they do not become macrophages.
n.1: Neutrophils are the most numerous WBCs and the first phagocytes at an infection, but they do not develop into macrophages.
n.3: Basophils are the least numerous WBCs and release histamine and heparin; they are not macrophage precursors.

q: A 25-year-old woman needs red blood cells immediately, before her blood type can be tested. Which donor type is the safest choice?
o: O positive
AB positive
O negative
AB negative
w: Type O negative red cells carry no A, B or Rh (D) antigens, so the recipient's antibodies have nothing to attack. O negative is the universal red-cell donor, and avoiding Rh exposure matters in a woman who may later become pregnant.

n.0: O positive cells carry the Rh (D) antigen, which could sensitize an Rh-negative woman.
n.1: AB positive is the universal recipient; its cells carry A, B and D antigens that most people's antibodies would attack.
n.3: AB negative cells carry A and B antigens, which would react with anti-A or anti-B in most recipients.

q: A patient with type A blood is mistakenly given type B red blood cells and has a transfusion reaction. What causes the reaction?
o: Her anti-B antibodies bind the B antigens on the donor red cells
Her plasma lacks antibodies, so the donor B antigens attack her cells
Her anti-A antibodies bind the A antigens on the donor red cells
Her A antigens bind directly to the B antigens on the donor red cells
w: Step 1: type A blood has A antigens on the cells and anti-B antibodies in the plasma. Step 2: donor type B cells carry B antigens, so her anti-B antibodies bind them and destroy the donor cells.

n.1: Type A plasma does contain antibodies (anti-B), and antigens are markers, not attackers.
n.2: Type A blood does not contain anti-A antibodies (they would attack her own cells), and type B cells carry no A antigen.
n.3: Antigens do not bind one another; antibodies bind antigens.

q: A runner moves to a high-altitude city where the air holds less oxygen, and over several weeks her red blood cell count rises. Which organ releases the hormone responsible?
o: The liver, which releases erythropoietin
Red bone marrow, which releases erythropoietin
The spleen, which releases erythropoietin
The kidneys, which release erythropoietin
w: Step 1: low blood oxygen is sensed by the kidneys. Step 2: the kidneys release erythropoietin (EPO), which stimulates red bone marrow to make more red blood cells.

n.0: The liver makes plasma proteins such as albumin; in adults, EPO comes from the kidneys.
n.1: Red bone marrow responds to EPO by making RBCs; it does not secrete the hormone.
n.2: The spleen removes old red blood cells; it does not release EPO.

q: Which plasma protein is the most abundant and is chiefly responsible for maintaining the osmotic pressure of the blood?
o: Fibrinogen
Hemoglobin
Albumin
Globulin
w: Albumin, made by the liver, is the most abundant plasma protein; it holds water in the blood vessels by osmotic pressure.

n.0: Fibrinogen is the clotting protein that becomes fibrin.
n.1: Hemoglobin is inside red blood cells, not a plasma protein.
n.3: Globulins include antibodies and transport proteins; they are less abundant than albumin.

q: Arterioles throughout the body constrict while cardiac output stays the same. What happens to blood pressure, and why?
o: It stays the same, because cardiac output is unchanged
It rises, because the stroke volume of the heart increases
It rises, because peripheral resistance increases
It falls, because less blood reaches the capillaries
w: Step 1: blood pressure depends on cardiac output and peripheral resistance. Step 2: arterioles control resistance, so narrowing them raises resistance; with cardiac output unchanged, blood pressure rises.

n.0: Pressure depends on resistance as well as cardiac output, so a rise in resistance raises it.
n.1: Stroke volume is unchanged here (cardiac output is the same); the rise comes from resistance.
n.3: Constriction raises arterial pressure even though capillary flow falls.

q: Blood is allowed to clot in a tube, and the clear fluid above the clot (serum) is collected. Which component of plasma is missing from the serum?
o: Glucose
Fibrinogen
Antibodies
Albumin
w: Serum is plasma without the clotting factors. Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin and used up in the clot, so it is absent from serum.

n.0: Glucose is a dissolved nutrient that stays in the serum.
n.2: Antibodies (globulins) are not used in clotting and remain in the serum.
n.3: Albumin does not take part in clotting, so it remains in the serum.

q: Swallowed food and inhaled air both travel through one region of the upper respiratory tract before their paths separate. Which structure is this shared passageway?
o: The trachea
The larynx
The pharynx
The nasal cavity
w: The pharynx (throat) is shared by the respiratory and digestive tracts: air passes on to the larynx, while food passes behind it into the esophagus.

n.0: The trachea carries air only, from the larynx to the main bronchi; it lies in front of the esophagus.
n.1: The larynx (voice box) carries air only; the epiglottis covers it during swallowing so food does not enter.
n.3: The nasal cavity warms, humidifies and filters inhaled air; food does not normally pass through it.

q: A toddler inhales a small bead, and an X-ray shows it lodged in one of the main bronchi. Which bronchus is it most likely in, and why?
o: The left, because it is wider and runs more vertically than the right
The right, because it is shorter, wider and more vertical than the left
The left, because the heart pushes the trachea toward the left side
The right, because it is narrower and so traps objects more easily
w: The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical than the left, so it continues almost straight down from the trachea and aspirated objects usually lodge there.

n.0: This describes the right main bronchus, not the left; the left is longer, narrower and angled more horizontally around the heart.
n.2: The heart sits to the left and makes the left bronchus angle away more sharply, which makes the left side the less likely site.
n.3: Right side is correct, but the reason is wrong: the right main bronchus is wider, not narrower.

q: The Adam's apple seen on the front of the neck is formed by which structure?
o: First cartilage ring of the trachea
Thyroid cartilage of the larynx
Thyroid gland over the trachea
Epiglottis at the top of the larynx
w: The Adam's apple is the shield-shaped thyroid cartilage, the largest cartilage of the larynx (voice box).

n.0: The tracheal rings lie below the larynx and form no visible prominence; the Adam's apple is laryngeal cartilage.
n.2: The thyroid gland is an endocrine gland lying over the trachea below the larynx; it shares a name with the thyroid cartilage but is a different structure.
n.3: The epiglottis is the flap that covers the larynx during swallowing; it sits behind the tongue and forms no bulge on the neck.

q: The airway is divided into a conducting zone and a respiratory zone. Which structure belongs to the respiratory zone?
o: Alveolar duct
Laryngopharynx
Terminal bronchiole
Segmental (tertiary) bronchus
w: The respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli) is where gas exchange occurs. Everything from the nose to the terminal bronchioles is conducting zone.

n.1: The laryngopharynx is part of the pharynx, high in the conducting zone and shared with food.
n.2: The terminal bronchiole is the last part of the conducting zone; gas exchange begins after it, at the respiratory bronchioles.
n.3: Segmental (tertiary) bronchi are cartilage-supported conducting airways with no gas exchange.

q: The trachea is held open by rings of hyaline cartilage that are incomplete on the posterior side. What is the main advantage of leaving the back of each ring open?
o: The open ends anchor the vocal cords inside the trachea
The esophagus behind it can expand as a swallowed bolus passes
The trachea can collapse completely during each quiet expiration
Gases can diffuse through the thin posterior wall into the blood
w: The C-shaped rings keep the trachea open for airflow, while the open back faces the esophagus so the esophagus can bulge forward as food passes down.

n.0: The vocal cords are in the larynx, above the trachea, not attached to tracheal rings.
n.2: The rings exist to stop the trachea from collapsing; it stays open in both inspiration and expiration.
n.3: No gas exchange occurs in the trachea; it is part of the conducting zone (anatomical dead space).

q: Years of smoking destroy many of the cilia that line a patient's bronchi. Which normal airway function is most directly impaired?
o: Sweeping mucus and trapped particles up toward the pharynx
Producing mucus from goblet cells to trap inhaled dust
Warming and humidifying air as it passes over the conchae
Secreting surfactant to keep the alveoli from collapsing
w: Cilia on the airway epithelium beat to move the mucus sheet, with its trapped particles, up toward the pharynx (the mucociliary escalator). Without cilia, mucus pools and is cleared by coughing.

n.1: Mucus is made by goblet cells, not cilia, so mucus is still produced; it is moving it that fails.
n.2: Warming and humidifying occur mainly in the nasal cavity, over the vascular mucosa of the conchae, not by bronchial cilia.
n.3: Surfactant is secreted by type II alveolar cells, which have no cilia.

q: Which type of epithelium lines most of the trachea and bronchi and carries the cilia of the mucociliary escalator?
o: Simple ciliated columnar epithelium
Ciliated simple cuboidal epithelium
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium
w: The conducting airways are lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells: one layer of cells that looks layered, with cilia that sweep mucus upward.

n.0: Simple ciliated columnar epithelium is a true single layer of tall cells that lines the uterine tubes; the trachea and bronchi have the pseudostratified form, whose nuclei sit at different heights.
n.1: Cuboidal cells, some with cilia, line only the smallest bronchioles near the respiratory zone, not the trachea and bronchi.
n.3: Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium resists abrasion in the oropharynx, laryngopharynx and esophagus; it has no cilia and does not line the trachea.

q: In an alveolus, which cell type secretes surfactant, and what does surfactant do?
o: Type II alveolar cells; it lowers surface tension so alveoli resist collapse
Type I alveolar cells; it lowers surface tension so alveoli resist collapse
Type II alveolar cells; it raises surface tension so alveoli recoil on expiration
Alveolar macrophages; it coats inhaled dust so the dust can be digested
w: Type II alveolar cells secrete surfactant, which lowers the surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli so they do not collapse at the end of each breath.

n.1: The effect is right but the cell is wrong: type I cells are thin squamous cells specialized for gas exchange.
n.2: The cell is right but the effect is reversed: surfactant decreases surface tension.
n.3: Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) engulf particles; they do not make surfactant.

q: A baby born at 26 weeks has not yet produced enough of the substance secreted by type II alveolar cells. Which problem is this baby most likely to have?
o: Mucus builds up in the bronchi because the cilia cannot beat effectively
Alveoli overinflate during each breath because surface tension stays too low
Alveoli collapse at the end of each breath because surface tension stays high
Inhaled dust builds up in the alveoli because too few dust cells are made
w: Step 1: type II alveolar cells make surfactant. Step 2: surfactant lowers surface tension; without enough of it, surface tension stays high and alveoli tend to collapse after each exhalation, making every breath hard work.

n.0: Moving mucus is the job of ciliated airway cells in the bronchi, not type II alveolar cells.
n.1: This reverses the effect: surfactant lowers surface tension, so a shortage leaves surface tension too high, not too low.
n.3: Dust cells are alveolar macrophages, which engulf particles; type II cells secrete surfactant, so a shortage of it does not reduce dust clearance.

q: Which statement correctly describes the pleural membranes and the fluid between them?
o: Parietal pleura covers each lung and visceral pleura lines the thoracic wall; the fluid lowers alveolar surface tension
Visceral pleura covers each lung and parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall; the fluid lowers alveolar surface tension
Visceral pleura covers each lung and parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall; the fluid reduces friction
Parietal pleura covers each lung and visceral pleura lines the thoracic wall; the fluid reduces friction
w: Visceral pleura covers the lung surface and parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall. Pleural fluid between them reduces friction and holds the lungs against the chest wall so they expand with it.

n.0: Both parts are wrong: visceral pleura is the layer on the lung, and lowering alveolar surface tension is the role of surfactant, not pleural fluid.
n.1: The membranes are named correctly, but lowering alveolar surface tension is the job of surfactant inside the alveoli; pleural fluid lies outside the lung and reduces friction.
n.3: The layers are reversed: visceral means on the organ (the lung), parietal means on the cavity wall.

q: A student rests a hand on her abdomen and feels it move outward during a normal, quiet inspiration. What is her diaphragm doing at that moment?
o: It relaxes and flattens, which lets the ribs fall and draws air in
It contracts, flattens and moves downward, enlarging the thoracic cavity
It contracts and domes upward, which pushes air into the lungs
It relaxes and domes upward, which enlarges the thoracic cavity
w: In inspiration the diaphragm contracts, flattens and moves down, increasing the vertical size of the thoracic cavity. The larger volume lowers pressure in the lungs, so air flows in.

n.0: A relaxed diaphragm domes upward rather than flattening, and falling ribs reduce thoracic volume.
n.2: A contracting diaphragm flattens and moves down; it does not dome upward or push air.
n.3: Relaxing and doming upward is what the diaphragm does in expiration, and it makes the thoracic cavity smaller.

q: When the volume of the thoracic cavity increases during inspiration, what happens to the pressure inside the lungs, and which way does air move?
o: Pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, so air flows in
Pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in
Pressure stays equal to atmospheric pressure as air flows in
Pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, so air flows out
w: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely related. Larger thoracic volume means lower intrapulmonary pressure; air flows from high (atmosphere) to low (lungs).

n.0: A larger volume lowers the pressure; higher pressure in the lungs would push air out.
n.2: Air moves only when a pressure gradient exists; equal pressures mean no airflow.
n.3: The pressure change is right, but air moves from high to low pressure, which is into the lungs.

q: Which statement best describes quiet expiration in a healthy adult at rest?
o: It is passive: the inspiratory muscles relax and the lungs recoil elastically
It is passive: the abdominal muscles relax and the diaphragm flattens out
It is active: the internal intercostals contract and pull the ribs down
It is active: the diaphragm contracts and pushes upward against the lungs
w: Quiet expiration is passive: the diaphragm and external intercostals relax, the elastic lungs and chest wall recoil, thoracic volume falls and pressure rises above atmospheric, so air flows out.

n.1: A flattening diaphragm enlarges the thorax, which belongs to inspiration, not expiration.
n.2: Internal intercostals are used in forced expiration (coughing, exercise), not quiet breathing.
n.3: The diaphragm relaxes during expiration; when it contracts it flattens downward.

q: A spinal cord injury high in the neck damages the nerve that supplies the main muscle of quiet breathing. Which nerve is it?
o: The vagus nerve
The accessory nerve
The intercostal nerves
The phrenic nerve
w: The phrenic nerve, which arises from the cervical spinal cord, supplies the diaphragm, the main muscle of breathing.

n.0: The vagus nerve (CN X) carries parasympathetic fibers to thoracic and abdominal organs; it does not drive the diaphragm.
n.1: The accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies neck and shoulder muscles such as the trapezius.
n.2: Intercostal nerves supply the intercostal muscles, which assist breathing but are not the main muscle.

q: A basic spirometer measures the air a person breathes in and out through a mouthpiece. Which lung volume cannot be measured directly with this device?
o: Inspiratory reserve volume
Residual volume
Vital capacity
Expiratory reserve volume
w: Residual volume is the air that remains in the lungs after the most forceful exhalation; because it is never breathed out, a simple spirometer cannot record it.

n.0: Inspiratory reserve volume is extra air inhaled beyond a normal breath and is measured by spirometry.
n.2: Vital capacity is the total that can be exhaled after a maximal breath, so it is measured directly.
n.3: Expiratory reserve volume is the extra air forced out after a normal exhalation, so the spirometer records it.

q: A spirometry report lists a vital capacity of 4,800 mL and a residual volume of 1,200 mL. What is this person's total lung capacity?
w: Total lung capacity = vital capacity + residual volume = 4,800 + 1,200 = 6,000 mL.

n.0: 4,800 mL is the vital capacity; it leaves out the residual volume that is always in the lungs.
n.1: 5,300 mL adds a 500 mL tidal volume, which is already included in vital capacity.
n.2: 3,600 mL subtracts residual volume instead of adding it.

q: During a hard cough or a forced exhalation, which muscles contract to push air out of the lungs?
o: The external intercostals and the diaphragm
The external intercostals and abdominal muscles
The diaphragm and the internal intercostals
The internal intercostals and abdominal muscles
w: Forced expiration is active: the internal intercostals pull the ribs down and the abdominal muscles push the abdominal organs up against the relaxed diaphragm, shrinking the thorax.

n.0: The external intercostals and diaphragm are the muscles of inspiration.
n.1: The abdominal muscles help, but the external intercostals lift the ribs for inspiration.
n.2: The internal intercostals help, but the diaphragm relaxes during expiration; contraction would enlarge the thorax.

q: A healthy adult's spirometry shows a tidal volume of 500 mL, an inspiratory reserve volume of 3,000 mL, an expiratory reserve volume of 1,100 mL and a residual volume of 1,200 mL. What is the vital capacity?
w: Vital capacity = tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume + expiratory reserve volume = 500 + 3,000 + 1,100 = 4,600 mL. Residual volume is not included because it cannot be exhaled.

n.0: 4,100 mL leaves out the tidal volume (3,000 + 1,100).
n.1: 5,800 mL adds the residual volume as well, which gives total lung capacity rather than vital capacity.
n.3: 3,500 mL is tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume only (the inspiratory capacity); the expiratory reserve volume is missing.

q: By what process do oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the respiratory membrane between the alveoli and the pulmonary capillaries?
o: Simple diffusion down their partial-pressure gradients
Osmosis driven by the solute concentration of plasma
Facilitated diffusion through protein gas channels
Active transport by carrier proteins that use ATP
w: O₂ and CO₂ are small, nonpolar gases that move across the thin respiratory membrane by simple diffusion, each from its higher partial pressure to its lower partial pressure. No energy is used.

n.1: Osmosis is the movement of water, not of dissolved gases.
n.2: Small nonpolar gases pass straight through the lipid bilayer without carrier or channel proteins.
n.3: Gas exchange needs no ATP; the gases move down their gradients, not against them.

q: In a healthy adult, how is most of the oxygen in arterial blood carried to the tissues?
o: Bound to hemoglobin inside red blood cells
Bound to albumin and other plasma proteins
As bicarbonate ions carried in the plasma
Dissolved directly in the plasma around the cells
w: About 98.5% of oxygen travels bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells as oxyhemoglobin; only about 1.5% is dissolved in plasma.

n.1: Albumin maintains osmotic pressure and carries some drugs and hormones; it is not an oxygen carrier.
n.2: Bicarbonate is the main carrier form of carbon dioxide, not oxygen.
n.3: Oxygen dissolves poorly in plasma, so only about 1.5% is carried this way.

q: Carbon dioxide produced by working muscle must be carried to the lungs. In which form is most of this carbon dioxide transported in the blood?
o: Bound to hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin
Bound to the iron atoms of heme groups
Dissolved as carbon dioxide gas in plasma
As bicarbonate ions in the plasma
w: About 70% of CO₂ is carried as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), formed inside red blood cells by carbonic anhydrase and then moved into the plasma. About 20-23% rides on hemoglobin and 7-10% is dissolved.

n.0: Carbaminohemoglobin carries only about a fifth of the CO₂, not most of it.
n.1: Iron in heme binds oxygen; CO₂ that binds hemoglobin attaches to the globin protein, and it is still the minority route.
n.2: Only about 7-10% of CO₂ is carried dissolved in plasma.

q: A stroke damages the region of the brain that generates the basic rhythm of breathing. Which region is damaged?
o: Hypothalamic nuclei
Pons
Cerebellar cortex
Medulla oblongata
w: The respiratory centers in the medulla oblongata set the basic breathing rhythm; the pons helps smooth the pattern.

n.0: The hypothalamus regulates temperature, hunger and thirst; it does not generate the breathing rhythm.
n.1: The pons modifies and smooths the breathing pattern, but the basic rhythm is generated in the medulla.
n.2: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance; it is not a breathing center.

q: In a healthy person at rest, which change in the blood is the strongest stimulus to increase the rate and depth of breathing?
o: A fall in oxygen, sensed by the central chemoreceptors
A fall in carbon dioxide, sensed as a rise in pH
A rise in oxygen, sensed by the carotid bodies
A rise in carbon dioxide, sensed as a fall in pH
w: Rising CO₂ is the main everyday drive to breathe. CO₂ forms carbonic acid, lowering the pH of cerebrospinal fluid, which central chemoreceptors in the medulla detect.

n.0: Low oxygen is a weaker, backup stimulus in healthy people, and it is sensed by peripheral chemoreceptors, not central ones.
n.1: Falling CO₂ and rising pH slow breathing rather than speed it up.
n.2: A rise in oxygen would not drive breathing up; the carotid bodies respond to a fall in O₂.

q: A hiker climbs to high altitude, where each breath holds less oxygen. Which receptors respond most directly to the drop in blood oxygen?
o: Central chemoreceptors on the surface of the medulla oblongata
Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies
Stretch receptors in the walls of the bronchioles
Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and the aortic arch
w: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies respond to low O₂ (and also to CO₂ and H⁺), signaling the medulla to increase ventilation.

n.0: Central chemoreceptors respond to CO₂ through the pH of cerebrospinal fluid, not to low oxygen.
n.2: Bronchiolar stretch receptors sense lung inflation, not blood oxygen.
n.3: Baroreceptors sense stretch from blood pressure, not oxygen levels.

q: A patient sedated after surgery breathes slowly and shallowly for over an hour. Which change in the patient's arterial blood is expected?
o: CO₂ falls and pH rises (respiratory alkalosis)
CO₂ rises and pH rises (respiratory alkalosis)
CO₂ falls and pH falls (respiratory acidosis)
CO₂ rises and pH falls (respiratory acidosis)
w: Step 1: hypoventilation removes too little CO₂, so CO₂ builds up. Step 2: CO₂ + H₂O forms carbonic acid, which releases H⁺, so pH falls: respiratory acidosis.

n.0: Falling CO₂ and rising pH follow hyperventilation, not slow shallow breathing.
n.1: CO₂ does rise, but extra CO₂ adds H⁺, which lowers pH rather than raising it.
n.2: Slow breathing retains CO₂, so CO₂ rises rather than falls.

q: During a panic attack, a student breathes rapidly and deeply for several minutes. Using CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, what happens in her blood?
o: CO₂ builds up, the reaction shifts right, H⁺ rises and pH falls
CO₂ is blown off, the reaction shifts left, H⁺ falls and pH rises
CO₂ is blown off, the reaction shifts right, H⁺ rises and pH falls
CO₂ is blown off, the reaction shifts left, H⁺ falls and pH falls
w: Step 1: hyperventilation removes CO₂ faster than it is made. Step 2: with less CO₂, the equilibrium shifts left, using up H⁺; fewer H⁺ ions means a higher pH (respiratory alkalosis).

n.0: CO₂ builds up with slow, shallow breathing, not with rapid deep breathing.
n.2: Removing a reactant (CO₂) shifts the equilibrium left, not right, so H⁺ falls.
n.3: The shift and the fall in H⁺ are right, but fewer H⁺ ions means pH rises.

q: Physiologists distinguish pulmonary ventilation, external respiration, internal respiration and cellular respiration. Which event is an example of internal respiration?
o: A mitochondrion uses oxygen to make ATP from glucose
Oxygen diffuses from an alveolus into a pulmonary capillary
Oxygen diffuses from a systemic capillary into a muscle cell
Air moves into the alveoli as the diaphragm contracts
w: Internal respiration is gas exchange between systemic capillary blood and body cells: O₂ diffuses into the cells and CO₂ diffuses out into the blood.

n.0: Using O₂ to make ATP is cellular respiration, a separate process inside the mitochondria.
n.1: Exchange between alveoli and pulmonary capillaries is external respiration.
n.3: Moving air into the lungs is pulmonary ventilation (breathing), not gas exchange.

q: Carbon dioxide entering the blood at the tissues is rapidly combined with water to form carbonic acid, which then releases bicarbonate. Where does the enzyme that speeds this reaction act?
o: Carbonic anhydrase inside red blood cells
Carbonic anhydrase dissolved in the plasma
Surfactant lining the alveolar walls
Hemoglobin inside the red blood cells
w: Carbonic anhydrase inside red blood cells catalyzes CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃. Carbonic acid releases H⁺ and HCO₃⁻, and most of the bicarbonate then moves out into the plasma for transport.

n.1: The bicarbonate ends up mostly in plasma, but the enzyme that makes it works inside red blood cells.
n.2: Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension and is not an enzyme for CO₂ conversion.
n.3: Hemoglobin carries O₂ and some CO₂ and buffers H⁺, but it is not the enzyme that forms carbonic acid.

q: Why does carbon monoxide poisoning reduce oxygen delivery to the tissues even when a person is breathing air with a normal oxygen content?
o: CO thickens the respiratory membrane, slowing O₂ diffusion into blood
CO dissolves in plasma and lowers the amount of O₂ plasma can hold
CO binds hemoglobin far more strongly than O₂, leaving fewer sites for O₂
CO converts bicarbonate to carbonic acid, making the blood too acidic
w: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does, so hemoglobin sites are occupied by CO and less O₂ can be carried, although lung oxygen levels are normal.

n.0: CO does not thicken the respiratory membrane; diffusion into the blood is not the problem.
n.1: Plasma carries only about 1.5% of oxygen, so this could not explain the large fall in delivery.
n.3: CO does not act on the bicarbonate system; its effect is on hemoglobin binding.

q: A student is sorting the body's defenses into categories for a study guide. Which of the following belongs in the first line of defense, the external barriers?
o: Complement proteins that lyse microbes
Interferons released by virus-infected cells
Lysozyme in tears and saliva
Neutrophils that engulf bacteria in the tissues
w: The first line of defense is the external barriers: intact skin, mucous membranes and mucus, cilia, stomach acid, and secretions such as tears and saliva that contain the antibacterial enzyme lysozyme.

n.0: Complement proteins circulate in the blood plasma, a second-line defense.
n.1: Interferons act inside the body after a virus has infected cells, a second-line defense.
n.3: Neutrophils are internal phagocytes, part of the second line of defense.

q: Within hours of bacteria entering a cut on the hand, white blood cells pour into the injured tissue. Which phagocytes typically arrive first and in the largest numbers?
o: Neutrophils
Natural killer cells
Dendritic cells
Macrophages
w: Neutrophils are the first phagocytes to arrive in large numbers at a site of bacterial infection. Monocytes follow and become macrophages.

n.1: NK cells kill virus-infected and tumor cells; they are not the phagocytes that clear bacteria from a wound.
n.2: Dendritic cells are phagocytes best known for presenting antigen to T cells; they are not the first wave that floods infected tissue.
n.3: Macrophages develop from monocytes that arrive after the neutrophils.

q: After a splinter pierces the skin, mast cells near the wound release histamine. Which effect of histamine directly produces the redness and swelling around the splinter?
o: Release of pyrogens that reset the hypothalamus
Vasodilation with decreased capillary permeability
Vasodilation with increased capillary permeability
Vasoconstriction with decreased capillary permeability
w: Histamine dilates local blood vessels (more blood flow: redness and heat) and makes capillaries leakier (fluid moves into the tissue: swelling). These changes also help phagocytes reach the site.

n.0: Pyrogens resetting the hypothalamus cause fever, a body-wide response, not local redness and swelling.
n.1: Vasodilation explains the redness, but the swelling needs increased permeability so fluid leaks into the tissue.
n.3: Vasoconstriction would reduce blood flow and redness; histamine dilates vessels.

q: A cell infected with a virus secretes proteins that diffuse to nearby cells and help those cells resist infection by the virus. Which innate defense does this describe?
o: Antibodies from plasma cells
Interferons
Histamine from mast cells
Complement proteins
w: Interferons are made by virus-infected cells and protect neighboring cells, an innate second-line defense.

n.0: Antibodies come from plasma cells in the adaptive response, not from the infected cell itself.
n.2: Histamine from mast cells drives inflammation; it does not help neighboring cells resist a virus.
n.3: Complement proteins circulate in plasma, lyse microbes and enhance phagocytosis; infected cells do not secrete them to protect their neighbors.

q: Which cell destroys virus-infected cells and tumor cells without needing prior exposure to a specific antigen, making it part of innate rather than adaptive immunity?
o: Cytotoxic (CD8) T cell
Natural killer cell
Helper (CD4) T cell
Plasma cell
w: Natural killer (NK) cells are innate defenders that kill virus-infected and tumor cells without prior exposure to the antigen.

n.0: Cytotoxic T cells also kill infected cells, but they must first be activated by a specific antigen, so they are adaptive.
n.2: Helper T cells coordinate the adaptive response; they do not kill cells directly.
n.3: Plasma cells secrete antibodies in the adaptive humoral response.

q: A patient with a bacterial infection develops a moderate fever. Which statement best describes how the fever arises and how it helps the body?
o: Histamine resets the hypothalamic set point, and moderate heat activates memory cells
Pyrogens reset the hypothalamic set point, and moderate heat inhibits pathogens
Pyrogens reset the pituitary set point, and moderate heat inhibits pathogens
Pyrogens reset the hypothalamic set point, giving an antigen-specific adaptive defense
w: Fever is an innate, nonspecific second-line defense. Pyrogens released during infection reset the temperature set point in the hypothalamus, and a moderate rise in body temperature inhibits pathogens.

n.0: Pyrogens, not histamine, reset the set point; histamine drives local inflammation, and memory cells belong to adaptive immunity.
n.2: The body's temperature set point is in the hypothalamus, not the pituitary.
n.3: Fever is innate and nonspecific; it does not target one antigen the way adaptive immunity does.

q: After a car accident, a patient's ruptured spleen is surgically removed. Which normal function is most directly lost along with the spleen?
o: Absorbing dietary fats through lacteals in the intestine
Filtering lymph before it returns to the bloodstream
Maturing T lymphocytes before they enter circulation
Filtering blood and removing worn-out red blood cells
w: The spleen, the largest lymphoid organ, filters blood rather than lymph: it removes old or damaged red blood cells and platelets and mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens.

n.0: Lacteals in the intestinal villi absorb dietary fats; the spleen has no part in fat absorption.
n.1: Filtering lymph is the job of the lymph nodes; the spleen filters blood.
n.2: T lymphocytes mature in the thymus, not the spleen.

q: Lymph collected from the left arm, the abdomen and both legs must return to the bloodstream. By which route does this lymph re-enter the blood?
o: Thoracic duct into the left subclavian vein
Right lymphatic duct into the right subclavian vein
Thoracic duct into the right subclavian vein
Thoracic duct into the superior vena cava
w: The thoracic duct drains most of the body, including both legs, the abdomen and the left arm, into the left subclavian vein. The right lymphatic duct drains the right arm and the right side of the head and thorax.

n.1: The right lymphatic duct drains the right arm and the right side of the head and thorax, not the left arm or the legs.
n.2: The thoracic duct joins the venous system on the left side, at the left subclavian vein.
n.3: The thoracic duct empties into the left subclavian vein, not directly into the superior vena cava.

q: Lymphatic vessels have no pump like the heart, yet lymph from the legs still moves steadily up toward the veins of the upper chest. Which mechanism keeps it moving one way?
o: Rhythmic pumping by the lymph nodes, with valves
Pressure from the right ventricle, with valves
Skeletal muscle and breathing movements, with valves
Suction as the spleen filters the lymph, with valves
w: Lymph is moved by the squeezing of skeletal muscles and the pressure changes of breathing; valves in the lymphatic vessels keep the flow one-way toward the subclavian veins.

n.0: Lymph nodes filter lymph and house lymphocytes and macrophages; they do not contract to pump it along.
n.1: The right ventricle pumps blood out to the lungs; it gives no push to lymph, which drifts through low-pressure vessels toward the veins.
n.3: The spleen filters blood, not lymph, and it does not draw lymph through the lymphatic vessels.

q: After several axillary lymph nodes are removed during breast cancer surgery, a patient develops lasting swelling of the arm on that side. Which lymphatic function best explains the swelling?
o: Filtering blood and removing worn-out red blood cells
Returning excess interstitial fluid to the blood
Absorbing dietary fats through lacteals in the villi
Filtering lymph to trap microbes before it reaches the blood
w: Lymphatic vessels collect excess interstitial fluid (lymph) and return it to the blood. Removing the axillary nodes disrupts drainage from the arm, so fluid builds up in the tissues.

n.0: Filtering blood and removing old red blood cells is a function of the spleen, not the axillary lymph nodes.
n.2: Lacteals absorb fats in the intestinal villi; they do not drain the arm.
n.3: The nodes do filter lymph, but losing that filter would raise infection risk; the swelling comes from fluid that is no longer drained.

q: During a humoral immune response to a bacterial toxin, which cells secrete large amounts of antibodies that circulate in the blood and lymph?
o: Cytotoxic T cells that recognize the toxin
Plasma cells derived from activated B cells
Helper T cells that coordinate the response
Memory B cells that persist after infection
w: Activated B cells divide and differentiate into plasma cells, which secrete antibodies, and memory B cells, which wait for a later exposure.

n.0: Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells directly in cell-mediated immunity; they do not make antibodies.
n.2: Helper T cells release cytokines that activate B cells, but they do not secrete antibodies.
n.3: Memory B cells give a faster response on re-exposure; the antibody-secreting cells are plasma cells.

q: Both B and T lymphocytes arise from stem cells in red bone marrow. Where does each type of lymphocyte complete its maturation before it can respond to antigens?
o: T cells in the thymus; B cells in red bone marrow
T cells in the lymph nodes; B cells in red bone marrow
T cells in the thymus; B cells in the spleen
T cells in red bone marrow; B cells in the thymus
w: T cells mature in the thymus (T for thymus), and B cells mature in red bone marrow. These are the two primary lymphoid organs.

n.1: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs that house mature lymphocytes; T cells mature in the thymus.
n.2: The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ where mature lymphocytes respond to antigens; B cells mature in red bone marrow.
n.3: This reverses the two sites: T cells mature in the thymus and B cells in red bone marrow.

q: In advanced HIV infection, both antibody production and cell-mediated killing become weak. Destruction of which cell type best explains the failure of both responses?
o: Natural killer cells
B lymphocytes
Helper (CD4) T cells
Cytotoxic (CD8) T cells
w: Two steps. (1) HIV destroys helper (CD4) T cells. (2) Helper T cells normally activate both B cells (antibody response) and cytotoxic T cells (cell-mediated response), so losing them weakens both arms of adaptive immunity.

n.0: NK cells are innate; losing them would not explain the failure of both adaptive responses.
n.1: Losing B cells would reduce antibodies but not cell-mediated killing; HIV targets helper T cells.
n.3: Losing cytotoxic T cells would weaken cell-mediated killing but would not explain the weak antibody response; HIV targets CD4 cells.

q: A newborn is protected against several infections for the first few months of life by antibodies received from the mother before birth. Which antibody class provides this protection?
o: IgA
IgM
IgE
IgG
w: IgG is the only antibody class that crosses the placenta, giving the fetus naturally acquired passive immunity that fades over weeks to months after birth.

n.0: IgA reaches the infant in breast milk after birth, not across the placenta before birth.
n.1: IgM is a large pentamer that does not cross the placenta; it is the first antibody made in a primary response.
n.2: IgE binds mast cells and basophils in allergy and parasite defense; it does not cross the placenta.

q: A child receives a booster dose of a vaccine one year after the first dose. Compared with the response to the first dose, how does the response to the booster differ?
o: Faster and stronger, mainly IgM, because memory cells already exist
Slower and weaker, because leftover antibodies block the antigen
Faster and stronger, mainly IgG, because memory cells already exist
Similar in speed, mainly IgM, because plasma cells must form again
w: The first dose triggers a primary response (a lag of days, mainly IgM) and leaves memory cells. On re-exposure, the memory cells drive a secondary response that is faster, stronger and longer lasting and is dominated by IgG. This is why booster doses work.

n.0: Faster and stronger is right, but the secondary response is mainly IgG; IgM dominates the primary response.
n.1: Memory cells make the secondary response faster and stronger, not slower and weaker.
n.3: Memory cells make the secondary response faster, and IgG rather than IgM dominates it.

q: Minutes after a bee sting, a student who was sensitized by an earlier sting develops hives and wheezing. Which antibody, bound to which cells, triggers this reaction?
o: IgE bound to neutrophils and macrophages
IgA bound to cells of mucous membranes
IgG bound to mast cells and basophils
IgE bound to mast cells and basophils
w: Allergy and anaphylaxis are IgE-mediated. IgE made after the first sting binds to mast cells and basophils; on re-exposure the allergen binds that IgE and the cells release histamine and other mediators. Severe anaphylaxis is treated with epinephrine.

n.0: IgE is right, but it binds mast cells and basophils, the histamine-releasing cells, not phagocytes.
n.1: IgA protects mucous membranes in secretions; it does not trigger allergic reactions.
n.2: IgG is the main antibody of secondary responses in the blood; the antibody that arms mast cells in allergy is IgE.

q: A hiker bitten by a rattlesnake is treated with antivenom, a preparation of ready-made antibodies against the venom. Which type of immunity does the antivenom provide?
o: Artificially acquired passive immunity, immediate but temporary
Artificially acquired passive immunity, immediate and long-lasting
Artificially acquired active immunity, slow to start but long-lasting
Naturally acquired passive immunity, immediate but temporary
w: Antivenom delivers ready-made antibodies by injection: artificial (a medical intervention) and passive (the hiker's own immune system did not make them). Passive immunity works at once but fades within weeks to months and leaves no memory cells.

n.1: Passive immunity creates no memory cells, so it is temporary rather than long-lasting.
n.2: Active immunity requires the body to make its own antibodies, as after a vaccine; antivenom supplies them ready-made.
n.3: Natural passive immunity comes from the mother (IgG across the placenta, IgA in breast milk), not from an injection.

q: Several weeks after a kidney transplant, the recipient's immune system begins attacking the donor organ. Which cells directly kill the transplanted kidney cells?
o: Helper (CD4) T cells
Antibody-secreting plasma cells
Cytotoxic (CD8) T cells
Regulatory T cells
w: Cytotoxic (CD8) T cells of cell-mediated immunity directly kill virus-infected cells, cancer cells and transplanted cells.

n.0: Helper T cells coordinate the attack through cytokines but do not kill the cells themselves.
n.1: Plasma cells secrete antibodies; they do not make direct cell-to-cell kills.
n.3: Regulatory T cells suppress immune responses; they would dampen rejection rather than carry it out.

q: Before helper T cells can respond to a new pathogen, other cells must display fragments of the pathogen's antigens on MHC proteins. Which cells perform this antigen presentation?
o: Helper T cells and cytotoxic T cells
Mast cells and basophils
Dendritic cells and macrophages
Plasma cells and natural killer cells
w: Antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells) take in antigens and display fragments on MHC proteins so that T cells can recognize them.

n.0: T cells are the cells that recognize presented antigen; they are not the antigen-presenting cells.
n.1: Mast cells and basophils release histamine in inflammation and allergy; they are not antigen-presenting cells.
n.3: Plasma cells secrete antibodies and NK cells kill infected cells; neither presents antigen to T cells.

q: Which of the following disorders results from the immune system attacking the body's own tissues?
o: Osteoarthritis of the knees
Hay fever triggered by pollen
Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Rheumatoid arthritis
w: In autoimmune disease the immune system attacks self antigens. In rheumatoid arthritis it attacks the synovial membranes of the joints. Other examples include type 1 diabetes, lupus, multiple sclerosis, Hashimoto's thyroiditis and Graves' disease.

n.0: Osteoarthritis is wear-and-tear breakdown of articular cartilage, not an immune attack; rheumatoid arthritis is the autoimmune joint disease.
n.1: Hay fever is an IgE-mediated allergy (hypersensitivity) to a foreign antigen, pollen, not an attack on self tissue.
n.2: Type 2 diabetes is caused by insulin resistance; it is type 1 diabetes in which the immune system destroys the pancreatic beta cells.
